citations.quote:
Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n,m,p\ge1$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$. A matrix is **Hurwitz** when every complex eigenvalue has strictly negative real part, as in [[def-hurwitz-matrix-and-continuous-lyapunov-equation]]. It is **Schur stable** when every complex eigenvalue has modulus strictly less than one.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **continuously stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Hurwitz. The pair $(A,C)$ is **continuously detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Hurwitz.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **discretely stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Schur stable. The pair $(A,C)$ is **discretely detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Schur stable. These are exact existential properties of the given finite matrices. A residual size or an approximate spectral estimate does not itself establish any of them.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space over $F$,
and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. If the characteristic polynomial of $T$ splits
over $F$, then $V$ has an orthonormal basis in which the matrix of $T$ is upper
triangular.

For compatible linear maps between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces,

$$\lVert ST\rVert\le \lVert S\rVert\,\lVert T\rVert.$$

For every such linear map $T$,

$$\lVert T^*T\rVert=\lVert T\rVert^2.$$

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.
Every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ splits over $\mathbb C$.

A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $F$ be a field and let $A\in M_n(F)$. If $n\geq1$, regard $xI_n-A$ as a matrix over the commutative polynomial ring $F[x]$. The **characteristic polynomial of $A$** is

$$\chi_A(x):=\det(xI_n-A)\in F[x].$$

For $n=0$, define the characteristic polynomial of the unique $0\times0$ matrix to be the constant polynomial $1$. This agrees with the empty-product convention and makes the characteristic polynomial monic of degree $0$ in the zero-sized case.

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

Let $V$ be a vector space over a field $F$ and let $T:V\to V$ be linear. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an **eigenvalue** of $T$ when there is a nonzero vector $v\in V$ such that

$$T(v)=\lambda v.$$

Such a vector is an **eigenvector belonging to $\lambda$**. The **eigenspace** belonging to $\lambda$ is

$$E_\lambda(T):=\ker(T-\lambda I_V)=\{v\in V:T(v)=\lambda v\}.$$

Thus $E_\lambda(T)$ is a linear subspace and always contains $0_V$, while $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue exactly when $E_\lambda(T)\ne\{0_V\}$. The **spectrum of $T$ over $F$** is

$$\sigma_F(T):=\{\lambda\in F:\lambda\text{ is an eigenvalue of }T\}.$$

In particular, the unique endomorphism of the zero space has empty spectrum.

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space,

$$\sigma_F(T)=\{\lambda\in F:\chi_T(\lambda)=0\}.$$

derivations.claim: If $n=0$, the unique endomorphism and every power of it is the zero map on the zero domain; its operator norm is zero, so the assertion holds with $C_r=0$. Assume now $n\ge1$ and regard a real matrix, if present, as a complex matrix. Its characteristic polynomial is a nonconstant complex polynomial, so [F5] and [F2] give $M=UTU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $T=D+N$, where $D$ is diagonal and $N$ is strictly upper triangular. Similar matrices have the same eigenvalues: $Mv=\lambda v$ is equivalent to $T(U^*v)=\lambda(U^*v)$. By [F7] and [F8], the eigenvalues are the diagonal entries of $T$; hence $\rho(M)=\max_i|T_{ii}|=\|D\|_2$, where the last equality follows directly from the Euclidean induced norm. Set $\rho=\rho(M)<r$. Each occurrence of $N$ in a product raises the row-to-column index, while $D$ preserves it, so every word containing at least $n$ copies of $N$ is zero.

Expand $(D+N)^k$ as the sum of noncommuting words. The terms with exactly $j$ copies of $N$ number $\binom{k}{j}$, vanish for $j\ge n$, and for $j<n$ have norm at most $\rho^{k-j}\|N\|_2^j$ by [F3] and $\|D\|_2=\rho$. Thus $\|T^k\|_2\le\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,n-1)}\binom{k}{j}\rho^{k-j}\|N\|_2^j.$ Because $U$ and $U^*$ preserve vector norms by [F6] and $U^*$ maps the unit sphere onto itself, the induced norm [F4] gives $\|M^k\|_2=\|UT^kU^*\|_2=\|T^k\|_2$.

If $\rho=0$, then $D=0$ and $T=N$, so $T^k=0$ for $k\ge n$; taking $C_r=\max_{0\le k<n}\|T^k\|_2r^{-k}$ proves the claim. If $0<\rho<r$, each fixed $j<n$ satisfies $\binom{k}{j}\rho^{k-j}\|N\|_2^j/r^k\le c_j k^j(\rho/r)^k$ for a finite $c_j$. The ratio of consecutive terms $k^j(\rho/r)^k$ tends to $\rho/r<1$, so this sequence is bounded. Summing its finitely many bounds over $0\le j<n$ gives a finite $C_r$ in step 2.1.

Both dimensions equal the number of pivots in any echelon form of $A$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map of vector spaces over $F$, with $V$

derivations.claim: Suppose $(A,B)$ is continuously stabilizable and fix its same-field feedback $K$ from [F1]. If for some $\lambda$ with $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$ the horizontal matrix $H_\lambda=[\lambda I-A\;B]$ has rank less than $n$, [F2] and [F3] applied over $\mathbb C$ to $H_\lambda^*$ give a nonzero $y\in\mathbb C^n$ with $y^*(\lambda I-A)=0$ and $y^*B=0$. By [A1], the same real or complex $K$ acts on this vector, so $y^*(A-BK)=\lambda y^*$. Thus $\det(\lambda I-(A-BK))=0$, contradicting that $A-BK$ is Hurwitz.

Suppose $(A,C)$ is continuously detectable and fix its same-field injection $L$ from [F1]. If $V_\lambda=\begin{bmatrix}\lambda I-A\\C\end{bmatrix}$ has rank less than $n$, rank-nullity over $\mathbb C$ gives a nonzero $x\in\mathbb C^n$ with $(\lambda I-A)x=0$ and $Cx=0$. Hence $(A-LC)x=\lambda x$, which contradicts that $A-LC$ is Hurwitz because $\operatorname{Re}\lambda\ge0$.

Suppose $(A,B)$ is discretely stabilizable and fix its same-field Schur feedback $K$ from [F1]. If $[\lambda I-A\;B]$ has rank less than $n$ for some $|\lambda|\ge1$, the same complex left-kernel argument as in step 1.1 gives a nonzero $y$ with $y^*(A-BK)=\lambda y^*$. Thus $\det(\lambda I-(A-BK))=0$, contradicting Schur stability.

Suppose $(A,C)$ is discretely detectable and fix its same-field Schur injection $L$ from [F1]. If the vertical matrix has rank less than $n$ for some $|\lambda|\ge1$, its complex kernel contains a nonzero $x$ and $Cx=0$, so $(A-LC)x=\lambda x$. This contradicts Schur stability.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $n,m,p\ge1$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, and $C\in F^{p\times n}$. A matrix is **Hurwitz** when every complex eigenvalue has strictly negative real part, as in [[def-hurwitz-matrix-and-continuous-lyapunov-equation]]. It is **Schur stable** when every complex eigenvalue has modulus strictly less than one.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **continuously stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Hurwitz. The pair $(A,C)$ is **continuously detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Hurwitz.

The pair $(A,B)$ is **discretely stabilizable** if some $K\in F^{m\times n}$ makes $A-BK$ Schur stable. The pair $(A,C)$ is **discretely detectable** if some $L\in F^{n\times p}$ makes $A-LC$ Schur stable. These are exact existential properties of the given finite matrices. A residual size or an approximate spectral estimate does not itself establish any of them.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, $C\in F^{p\times n}$, and $R=R^*\in F^{m\times m}$ be positive definite. Write $Q=C^*C$ and $G=BR^{-1}B^*$. The inverse $R^{-1}$ is well-defined: [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]] supplies an invertible factor $R=LL^*$, so $R^{-1}=L^{-*}L^{-1}$. Thus $v^*Gv=\|L^{-1}B^*v\|_2^2\ge0$ and $v^*Qv=\|Cv\|_2^2\ge0$. The symbol $^*$ is transpose over $\mathbb R$ and conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$.

The **continuous algebraic Riccati equation (CARE)** is
$$A^*X+XA-XGX+Q=0.$$
Its residual is $F_c(X)=A^*X+XA-XGX+Q$, its feedback is $K_c(X)=R^{-1}B^*X$, and its closed-loop matrix is $A_c(X)=A-BK_c(X)=A-GX$.

For $X=X^*\succeq0$, $S_X:=R+B^*XB$ is positive definite because
$v^*S_Xv=v^*Rv+(Bv)^*X(Bv)>0$ for every nonzero $v$. The **discrete
algebraic Riccati equation (DARE)** is
$$X=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA.$$
Its residual is $F_d(X)=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA-X$. Whenever $X=X^*$, the matrix $R+B^*XB$ is positive definite if $X\succeq0$. Its feedback and closed-loop matrix are
$$K_d(X)=(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA,\qquad A_c(X)=A-BK_d(X).$$
A CARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian and $A_c(X)$ is Hurwitz. A DARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian, $R+B^*XB\succ0$, and $A_c(X)$ is Schur stable. No inverse of $A$ is part of either definition.

For Hermitian $X$ with $S_X$ invertible, multiplication gives
$$(I+GX)^{-1}=I-BS_X^{-1}B^*X,\qquad X(I+GX)^{-1}=X-XB S_X^{-1}B^*X.$$
In either product, the additional coefficient of $B$ is
$R^{-1}-S_X^{-1}-S_X^{-1}(B^*XB)R^{-1}=0$, because
$S_X=R+B^*XB$. Thus the DARE is equivalently
$X=Q+A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}A$, and its closed-loop matrix is
$A_c(X)=(I+GX)^{-1}A$.

The associated homogeneous symplectic pencil is
$$N=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\-Q&I\end{bmatrix},\qquad M=\begin{bmatrix}I&G\\0&A^*\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathcal P(\alpha,\beta)=\beta N-\alpha M.$$
The homogeneous-coordinate convention is that a finite eigenvalue
$\lambda$ is $[\alpha:\beta]=[\lambda:1]$ and $[1:0]$ denotes infinity.

Let $n\ge 1$ and let $A\in M_n(\mathbb C)$, with the real case obtained by
restricting scalars to $\mathbb R$. Then the following are equivalent:

1. $A$ has a Cholesky factorisation $A=LL^*$ with $L$ lower triangular and
   positive real diagonal.
2. $A$ is Hermitian positive definite.

When these conditions hold, the factor $L$ is unique.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$ be continuous and locally Lipschitz in the state variable, and let $(t_0,x_0)\in D$. Then a unique local solution of the IVP exists on some interval around the initial time. More quantitatively, if $h,r>0$ make

$$[t_0-h,t_0+h]\times\overline B(x_0,r)\subseteq D,$$

if $\|F\|_2\le M$ and $F$ has state-Lipschitz constant $L$ on this cylinder, and if $hM\le r$ and $Lh<1$, then there is exactly one solution on $[t_0-h,t_0+h]$ through $(t_0,x_0)$ whose graph lies in the cylinder. Any two solutions through the same initial data agree on every common subinterval containing $t_0$.

In particular, a unique local solution exists on an interval around the initial time.

Every initial value problem satisfying the Picard-Lindelof hypotheses has a unique maximal solution. Its domain is an open interval containing the initial time, and every other solution through the same data is its restriction.

Let $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be Hurwitz, let $\alpha=-\max\{\operatorname{Re}\lambda:\lambda\in\sigma(A)\}>0$, and write $e^{tA}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}t^kA^k/k!$. If $A=UTU^*$ is a unitary Schur triangularization and $T=D+N$ with $D$ diagonal and $N$ strictly upper triangular, then for every $t\ge0$,

$$
\|e^{tA}\|_2\le e^{-\alpha t}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{(t\|N\|_2)^k}{k!}.
$$

For real Hurwitz $A$, the same bound holds for its real matrix exponential, with the complex operator norm of its realification equal to the real one.

Let $I=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty compact interval, let
$C:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ be continuous, let $t_0\in I$, and let
$Y_0\in M_n(\mathbb R)$. For $n=0$, there is exactly one map $Y:I\to M_0(\mathbb R)$, namely the empty-matrix map, and all entrywise differential identities are vacuous. For $n\ge1$ and $a<b$, the linear matrix initial value problem

$$Y'(t)=C(t)Y(t),\qquad Y(t_0)=Y_0,$$

has a unique solution on all of $I$, with domain-relative one-sided
derivatives at the endpoints. If $n\ge1$ and $a=b$, then $t_0=a$ and there is exactly
one map $Y:I\to M_n(\mathbb R)$ with $Y(a)=Y_0$. This singleton map
extends to a solution of $Z'=C(a)Z$, $Z(a)=Y_0$, on an open interval
around $a$; any two such local continuations agree on their common interval
containing $a$. No time derivative or IVP solution on the singleton itself
is asserted.

derivations.claim: By [F3], $R^{-1}$ exists and $G=G^*\succeq0$, since $v^*Gv=(B^*v)^*R^{-1}(B^*v)\ge0$. Regard the Hermitian matrices as a finite-dimensional real vector space and solve the initial-value problem $P'(s)=A^*P(s)+P(s)A-P(s)GP(s)+Q,\qquad P(0)=0.$ Its polynomial vector field is locally Lipschitz: on each bounded matrix ball, expanding the quadratic difference gives $PGP-HGH=(P-H)GP+HG(P-H)$, which is bounded linearly in $\|P-H\|_F$. Thus [F4] and [F5] give a unique maximal solution. The adjoint $P(s)^*$ satisfies the same IVP, so uniqueness makes $P(s)=P(s)^*$ on its interval.

Fix $T$ in this interval and let $x$ follow any admissible control on $[0,T]$. Put $S(t)=P(T-t)$. Differentiating $x(t)^*S(t)x(t)$ and substituting the ODE gives $x^*Qx+u^*Ru+\frac{d}{dt}(x^*Sx)=(u+R^{-1}B^*Sx)^*R(u+R^{-1}B^*Sx).$ Integrating, using $P(0)=0$, yields $J_T(u)=x_0^*P(T)x_0+\int_0^T(u+R^{-1}B^*Sx)^*R(u+R^{-1}B^*Sx)\,dt.$ The candidate feedback makes $\dot x=(A-GS(t))x$, whose coefficient is continuous on $[0,T]$. If $F=\mathbb R$, [F7] gives its unique solution on the interval. If $F=\mathbb C$, write $x$ in real and imaginary parts and replace the coefficient $M$ by $\begin{bmatrix}\operatorname{Re}M&-\operatorname{Im}M\\\operatorname{Im}M&\operatorname{Re}M\end{bmatrix}$; [F7] applies to this continuous real system, and its solution is exactly the complex feedback trajectory. Thus $u=-R^{-1}B^*Sx$ is admissible and makes the last integral zero, so $x_0^*P(T)x_0$ is the finite-horizon value and $P(T)\succeq0$.

By stabilizability [F1], choose $K_0$ with $A_0=A-BK_0$ Hurwitz. Under $u=-K_0x$, [F6] bounds $x(t)=e^{tA_0}x_0$ by a square-integrable polynomial-exponential multiple of $\|x_0\|$. The control $K_0x(t)$ has the same property, so its cost on $[0,T]$ is at most $c\|x_0\|^2$ for one finite $c$ independent of $T$. Step 2.1 therefore gives $0\preceq P(T)\preceq cI$. If the maximal interval ended at finite $T_*$, the polynomial ODE field would be bounded on this bounded range, so $P'(s)$ would be bounded and every entry of $P(s)$ would have a finite limit as $s\uparrow T_*$. Applying [F4] at that limiting matrix extends the solution past $T_*$, contradicting maximality [F5]. Hence $P$ exists for every $s\ge0$.

For $T_2>T_1$, every control on $[0,T_2]$ has nonnegative cost after $T_1$; its restriction to $[0,T_1]$ costs at least $x_0^*P(T_1)x_0$ by step 2.1. Taking infima gives $P(T_2)\succeq P(T_1)$. Together with the bound in step 3.1, each quadratic form $v^*P(T)v$ increases to a finite limit. Applying this to the coordinate vectors and their pairwise sums shows every matrix entry converges to a Hermitian limit $X\succeq0$.

Let $\Phi(P)=A^*P+PA-PGP+Q$. By step 4.1 and continuity, $P'(T)=\Phi(P(T))\to\Phi(X)$. If $\Phi(X)\ne0$, polarization gives a vector $v$ with $v^*\Phi(X)v\ne0$. Then the derivative of the convergent scalar function $v^*P(T)v$ tends to a nonzero real number, so it is eventually bounded away from zero with constant sign; integration contradicts its convergence. Thus $\Phi(X)=0$, so $X$ solves the CARE.

Set $K=R^{-1}B^*X$ and $A_c=A-BK=A-GX$. The CARE gives $A_c^*X+XA_c=-Q-K^*RK$. Along $\dot x=A_cx$, integration over $[0,T]$ gives $\int_0^T(\|Cx(t)\|_2^2+u(t)^*Ru(t))\,dt=x_0^*Xx_0-x(T)^*Xx(T)\le x_0^*Xx_0.$ The Cholesky factor $R=LL^*$ is invertible by [F3], so $u^*Ru=\|L^*u\|_2^2$ controls $\|u\|_2^2$ by the finite operator norm of $L^{-*}$. Hence $Cx,u\in L^2(0,\infty)$.

By detectability [F1], choose $L$ with $A_o=A-LC$ Hurwitz. Then $\dot x=A_ox+w$, where $w=Bu+LCx\in L^2$. Since $x$ is locally absolutely continuous, $w$ is locally integrable and the product rule gives $\frac{d}{dt}(e^{-tA_o}x(t))=e^{-tA_o}w(t)$ almost everywhere. Integrating this identity from $0$ to $t$ and multiplying by $e^{tA_o}$ proves $x(t)=e^{tA_o}x_0+\int_0^t e^{(t-s)A_o}w(s)\,ds$. From [F6], there are $M,\alpha>0$ with $\|e^{tA_o}\|_2\le Me^{-\alpha t}$ after absorbing the finite polynomial factor into a smaller exponential rate. The initial term tends to zero. For the integral, split at a fixed $S$: the portion $0\le s\le S$ tends to zero as $t\to\infty$; by Cauchy–Schwarz the tail is at most $M(2\alpha)^{-1/2}\|w\|_{L^2(S,\infty)}$, which tends to zero as $S\to\infty$. Thus $x(t)\to0$. Since this holds for every initial state, no eigenvalue of $A_c$ can have nonnegative real part: an eigenvector for such an eigenvalue would not decay. Therefore $A_c$ is Hurwitz.

For any admissible control of finite infinite-horizon cost, $u,Cx\in L^2$. Repeating the stable-convolution argument in step 7.1 gives $x(T)\to0$. The same square-completion identity as step 2.1, now with constant $S=X$, yields $J_T(u)=x_0^*Xx_0-x(T)^*Xx(T)+\int_0^T(u+Kx)^*R(u+Kx)\,dt.$ Taking $T\to\infty$ gives $J_\infty(u)\ge x_0^*Xx_0$. The feedback in step 6.1 has $u+Kx=0$ and $x(T)\to0$, hence attains equality.

Let $Y\succeq0$ be any other CARE solution. Repeating steps 6.1–7.1 with $Y$ proves $A_Y=A-GY$ is Hurwitz. Subtracting the CAREs and using $XGX-YGY=PG(X-Y)+(X-Y)GY\quad\text{with }P=X$ gives $A_c^*(X-Y)+(X-Y)A_Y=0$. Hence the derivative of $e^{tA_c^*}(X-Y)e^{tA_Y}$ is zero, so this matrix equals $X-Y$ for every $t\ge0$. Both exponential factors tend to zero by [F6], forcing $X-Y=0$. Thus $X$ is the unique positive-semidefinite solution, and in particular the unique stabilizing one.

Polynomial ODE is Lipschitz on bounded sets; finite-horizon square completion gives PSD and a uniform stabilizing-feedback bound, hence global extension. Monotone quadratic forms polarize to a matrix limit; convergence of the derivative to the residual forces residual zero. Detectable stable convolution maps finite-cost L2 forcing to a decaying state, proving both stability and transversality for arbitrary finite-cost controls. derivations.claim: Define $P_0=0$ and recursively $S_j=R+B^*P_jB,\quad K_j=S_j^{-1}B^*P_jA,\quad P_{j+1}=Q+A^*P_jA-A^*P_jB S_j^{-1}B^*P_jA.$ If $P_j\succeq0$, then for nonzero $v$, $v^*S_jv=v^*Rv+(Bv)^*P_j(Bv)>0$, so $S_j^{-1}$ exists. For each $x,u$, expansion and completion of the positive square gives $x^*Qx+u^*Ru+(Ax+Bu)^*P_j(Ax+Bu)=x^*P_{j+1}x+(u+K_jx)^*S_j(u+K_jx).$ Thus $x^*P_{j+1}x$ is the finite-horizon value for $j+1$ stages, attained by the minimizing first control; induction gives $P_j\succeq0$.

For positive-semidefinite $P,Q$, if $(I+PQ)v=0$, multiplication by $v^*Q$ gives $v^*Qv+(Qv)^*P(Qv)=0$. Both terms are nonnegative, so [F5] gives $Qv=0$ and then $v=0$. Interchanging $P,Q$ proves the same for $I+QP$. Thus $I+YG$, $I+GY$, $I+GZ$, and $I+ZG$ are injective and hence invertible by [F6]. Since $(I+YG)Y=Y(I+GY)$, multiplication by the established inverses gives $(I+YG)^{-1}Y=Y(I+GY)^{-1}$. Further, multiplying both sides of $Y(I+GY)^{-1}-Z(I+GZ)^{-1}=(I+YG)^{-1}(Y-Z)(I+GZ)^{-1}$ by $I+YG$ on the left and $I+GZ$ on the right reduces both sides to $Y-Z$. Substitution into $f(Y)-f(Z)$ proves the difference identity in the Statement.

Longer horizons add nonnegative stage costs, so their value matrices increase in the Loewner order: $0\preceq P_j\preceq P_{j+1}$. By stabilizability [F1], choose $K_0$ so $A_0=A-BK_0$ is Schur stable. Under that fixed feedback the cost is bounded by $\sum_{k\ge0}(\|C\|_2^2+\|K_0^*RK_0\|_2)\|A_0^kx_0\|_2^2\le c\|x_0\|_2^2,$ because [F3] gives a summable geometric-square bound. Therefore $P_j\preceq cI$. The forms on $e_i$, $e_i+e_j$, and $e_i+\mathrm i e_j$ are bounded and monotone; they determine the diagonal entries and the real and imaginary parts of each Hermitian off-diagonal entry. Thus all entries converge to a Hermitian $X\succeq0$.

The update map is continuous on $P\succeq0$: $R+B^*PB\succeq R\succ0$, so its inverse varies continuously there. Passing to the limit in step 1.1 gives the DARE for $X$, and the same inequality gives $R+B^*XB\succ0$.

Put $S=R+B^*XB$, $K=S^{-1}B^*XA$, and $A_c=A-BK$. The square identity in step 1.1 with $P_j=X$ yields $x^*Qx+u^*Ru+(Ax+Bu)^*X(Ax+Bu)-x^*Xx=(u+Kx)^*S(u+Kx).$ For $u=-Kx$, summing from $k=0$ to $N-1$ gives total stage cost $x_0^*Xx_0-x_N^*Xx_N\le x_0^*Xx_0$. Thus $u,Cx\in\ell^2$.

By detectability [F1], choose $L$ such that $A_o=A-LC$ is Schur stable. Along the feedback trajectory, $x_{k+1}=A_ox_k+w_k,\qquad w_k=Bu_k+LCx_k\in\ell^2.$ Variation of constants gives $x_k=A_o^kx_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}A_o^{k-1-j}w_j$. The first term tends to zero by [F3]. For any fixed $J$, the finite sum over $j<J$ also tends to zero. The remaining sum is bounded by $\Big(\sum_{\ell\ge0}\|A_o^\ell\|_2^2\Big)^{1/2}\Big(\sum_{j\ge J}\|w_j\|_2^2\Big)^{1/2}.$ The first factor is finite by [F3], and the second tends to zero as $J\to\infty$. Hence $x_k\to0$. This holds for every initial state, so no eigenvalue of $A_c$ can satisfy $|\lambda|\ge1$; therefore $A_c$ is Schur stable.

For any finite-cost control, $u,Cx\in\ell^2$; the same detectability argument in step 5.1, now with its state equation, gives $x_k\to0$. Input $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, dimensions $n,m,p\ge1$, standard DARE data $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, $C\in F^{p\times n}$, and $R\in F^{m\times m}$ with $R=R^*\succ0$, a nonnegative integer iteration budget $N$, and the operationwise arithmetic/range controller. In finite mode the stored input entries are exact dyadics; also supply stored dyadic inverse and solution proposals for every recurrence and residual solve. In exact mode set $G_0=BR^{-1}B^*$, $H_0=Q=C^*C$, and $A_0=A$, the standard DARE coefficients of [[def-standard-continuous-and-discrete-riccati-equations]].

For finite-mode initialization, first solve $RV=B^*$ by the exact complete-pivoting elimination rule below, using order $m$ and the $n$ right-hand sides of $B^*$ in place of $M_j$ and $I$. Perform this preprocessing in exact rational arithmetic on the dyadic inputs. Form $BV$ and $C^*C$ exactly, then round each real and imaginary component once to the declared stored format (nearest, with ties to even), obtaining stored $G_0$ and $H_0$; set stored $A_0=A$. A zero pivot returns `inverse-inconclusive`; a component outside the controller's admitted range returns `range-failure`. On an initialization failure return the inputs, zero completed updates, any formed initial matrices and solve data, and unavailable for every unformed matrix or diagnostic. The finite-mode notation $G_0,H_0$ denotes these rounded matrices, not an assertion that $BR^{-1}B^*$ is dyadic. Record $V$ and the initialization rounding differences separately. This exact rational preprocessing has no asserted bit-cost bound and adds no point-certifier calls.

In exact mode, for each $j=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $M_j=I+G_jH_j$ and solve $M_jW_j=I$ by Gaussian elimination with complete pivoting: at stage $k$, scan the remaining submatrix, choose a nonzero entry of largest exact modulus with lexicographic tie-breaking, swap its row and column into pivot position, eliminate below it, and back-substitute for all columns of $I$, undoing the accumulated column permutation in the solution. If the remaining submatrix is exactly zero before all pivots, return `inverse-inconclusive`. This is a finite exact-arithmetic procedure; no bit-complexity bound is asserted.

In finite arithmetic, form the stored dyadic matrix $\widehat M_j=\operatorname{fl}(I+G_jH_j)$. For each standard basis vector $e_k$, call [[alg-point-verified-linear-system-certifier]] with $(\widehat M_j,e_k,R_j,\widehat w_{j,k})$, using the supplied stored dyadic inverse and solution proposals. Assemble the returned solution centers as $\widehat W_j$. If any call returns `range-failure`, return `range-failure`; if any call is `inconclusive`, return `inverse-inconclusive`; otherwise apply the recurrence updates below using $\widehat W_j$ and the declared operationwise arithmetic. The point certifier's solution balls are diagnostics for the stored solve and do not make the rounded recurrence an exact PSD-preserving recurrence.

In exact mode let $W_j$ be the exact solve result; in finite mode let $W_j=\widehat W_j$. The recurrence formulas are
$$
A_{j+1}=A_jW_jA_j,\qquad G_{j+1}=G_j+A_jW_jG_jA_j^*,\qquad H_{j+1}=H_j+A_j^*H_jW_jA_j.
$$
These formulas use no inverse of $A_j$. Any range failure while forming a stored matrix or applying an update returns `range-failure` with the current raw matrices.

After successful initialization, if all $N$ updates finish without a recurrence failure, return `budget-exhausted` with $N$ completed updates, including when $N=0$. This status records only completion of the prescribed budget; the diagnostics below remain required.

At initialization and after each update, preserve the raw matrices and report $\|G_j-G_j^*\|_F$ and $\|H_j-H_j^*\|_F$. To report the standard DARE residual, form $S_j=R+B^*H_jB$ exactly from the current $H_j$ and original input entries. In exact mode, $S_j$ need not be dyadic: independently solve $S_jV_j=I$ by the same exact elimination rule, using order $m$, and evaluate the residual from [[def-standard-continuous-and-discrete-riccati-equations]] exactly using $V_j$. In finite mode, $S_j$ is dyadic because the original inputs and current stored $H_j$ are dyadic; apply the point-certified solve rule to its $m$ columns with the separate residual proposal packet, and outward-evaluate the residual over the certified solution balls. If the residual solve or evaluation is unavailable or inconclusive, mark the residual unavailable without changing the recurrence status. Symmetrization may be used only to form a candidate and must be followed by fresh residual and positivity checks. On every exit return the current raw matrices, status, completed updates, symmetry defects, and available residual and solve certificates. No exact positive-semidefinite or structure-preserving backward-error claim is made from a rounded recurrence alone.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, $C\in F^{p\times n}$, and $R=R^*\in F^{m\times m}$ be positive definite. Write $Q=C^*C$ and $G=BR^{-1}B^*$. The inverse $R^{-1}$ is well-defined: [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]] supplies an invertible factor $R=LL^*$, so $R^{-1}=L^{-*}L^{-1}$. Thus $v^*Gv=\|L^{-1}B^*v\|_2^2\ge0$ and $v^*Qv=\|Cv\|_2^2\ge0$. The symbol $^*$ is transpose over $\mathbb R$ and conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$.

The **continuous algebraic Riccati equation (CARE)** is
$$A^*X+XA-XGX+Q=0.$$
Its residual is $F_c(X)=A^*X+XA-XGX+Q$, its feedback is $K_c(X)=R^{-1}B^*X$, and its closed-loop matrix is $A_c(X)=A-BK_c(X)=A-GX$.

For $X=X^*\succeq0$, $S_X:=R+B^*XB$ is positive definite because
$v^*S_Xv=v^*Rv+(Bv)^*X(Bv)>0$ for every nonzero $v$. The **discrete
algebraic Riccati equation (DARE)** is
$$X=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA.$$
Its residual is $F_d(X)=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA-X$. Whenever $X=X^*$, the matrix $R+B^*XB$ is positive definite if $X\succeq0$. Its feedback and closed-loop matrix are
$$K_d(X)=(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA,\qquad A_c(X)=A-BK_d(X).$$
A CARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian and $A_c(X)$ is Hurwitz. A DARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian, $R+B^*XB\succ0$, and $A_c(X)$ is Schur stable. No inverse of $A$ is part of either definition.

For Hermitian $X$ with $S_X$ invertible, multiplication gives
$$(I+GX)^{-1}=I-BS_X^{-1}B^*X,\qquad X(I+GX)^{-1}=X-XB S_X^{-1}B^*X.$$
In either product, the additional coefficient of $B$ is
$R^{-1}-S_X^{-1}-S_X^{-1}(B^*XB)R^{-1}=0$, because
$S_X=R+B^*XB$. Thus the DARE is equivalently
$X=Q+A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}A$, and its closed-loop matrix is
$A_c(X)=(I+GX)^{-1}A$.

The associated homogeneous symplectic pencil is
$$N=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\-Q&I\end{bmatrix},\qquad M=\begin{bmatrix}I&G\\0&A^*\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathcal P(\alpha,\beta)=\beta N-\alpha M.$$
The homogeneous-coordinate convention is that a finite eigenvalue
$\lambda$ is $[\alpha:\beta]=[\lambda:1]$ and $[1:0]$ denotes infinity.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

derivations.claim: If $(I+GH)v=0$, then multiplication by $v^*H$ gives $v^*Hv+(Hv)^*G(Hv)=0.$ Both terms are nonnegative, so $Hv=0$ and then $v=0$. Thus $I+GH$ is invertible; the same argument applies to $I+HG$. The identities $(I+GH)^{-1}G=G(I+HG)^{-1} =G^{1/2}(I+G^{1/2}HG^{1/2})^{-1}G^{1/2},$ $H(I+GH)^{-1}=(I+HG)^{-1}H =H^{1/2}(I+H^{1/2}GH^{1/2})^{-1}H^{1/2}$ follow by multiplication and the push-through identity. Their middle matrices are positive definite, so both displayed products are Hermitian positive semidefinite. Therefore the updates in [F1] give $G_1,H_1\succeq0$ and use only an inverse already proved to exist.

For any invertible displayed factors, direct multiplication gives the resolvent identity $\Phi_G(X)-\Phi_G(Y)=(I+XG)^{-1}(X-Y)(I+GY)^{-1},$ and the push-through identity $(I+UV)^{-1}U=U(I+VU)^{-1}$. For $X\succ0$, $\Phi_G(X)^{-1}=X^{-1}+G$. Put $U=\Phi_G(X)$ and $Y=A^*UA$. Applying the resolvent identity at $H+Y$ and $H$ gives $\Phi_G(H+Y)-\Phi_G(H)=(I+(H+Y)G)^{-1}Y(I+GH)^{-1}.$ Since $I+(H+Y)G=(I+HG)+YG$, multiplication verifies $(I+(H+Y)G)^{-1}Y=(I+HG)^{-1}Y\bigl(I+G(I+HG)^{-1}Y\bigr)^{-1}.$ Substituting $Y=A^*UA$ and applying push-through twice rewrites this difference as $(I+HG)^{-1}A^*\bigl(U^{-1}+AG(I+HG)^{-1}A^*\bigr)^{-1}A(I+GH)^{-1}.$ Using $U^{-1}=X^{-1}+G$ and [F1], the middle inverse is $X(I+G_1X)^{-1}$. Now $f(f(X))-H_1=A^*\bigl(\Phi_G(H+Y)-\Phi_G(H)\bigr)A$. Its left factor is $A^*(I+HG)^{-1}A^*=A_1^*$ and its right factor is $A(I+GH)^{-1}A=A_1$. Adding $H_1=H+A^*\Phi_G(H)A$ proves the composition formula for $X\succ0$.

For singular $X\succeq0$, replace it by $X+\varepsilon I$ in step 1.2 and let $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Step 1.1 guarantees every $I+G(X+\varepsilon I)$ and $I+G_1(X+\varepsilon I)$ is invertible; matrix inversion is continuous at these invertible limits. Hence the composition identity extends to every $X\succeq0$, including singular $A$ and singular $X$. By induction on $j$, the updated Riccati map is $f^{2^j}$ and its value at zero is $H_j$.

derivations.claim: Block multiplication gives $H\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}A-GX\\-Q-A^*X\end{bmatrix}.$ By [F1], $-Q-A^*X=XA-XGX=X(A-GX)$, proving the graph identity.

Set $T_X=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\X&I\end{bmatrix}$, whose inverse is $\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\-X&I\end{bmatrix}$. Using [F1], $T_X^{-1}HT_X=\begin{bmatrix}A-GX&-G\\0&-(A-GX)^*\end{bmatrix}.$ The eigenvalues of the first diagonal block lie in the open left half-plane by [F1]. If $\lambda$ is a root of its characteristic polynomial, then $-\overline\lambda$ is a root of the characteristic polynomial of $-(A-GX)^*$, since $\det(-\overline\lambda I+(A-GX)^*)=\overline{\det(-\lambda I+(A-GX))}=0$; these reflected roots lie in the open right half-plane. By [F5] each diagonal characteristic polynomial has degree $n$ and splits into $n$ roots counted with algebraic multiplicity. The characteristic polynomial factorization [F3] and root/eigenvalue connection [F4] therefore give exactly $n$ eigenvalues of $H$ in each open half-plane and none on the imaginary axis.  The first coordinate subspace is invariant and its restriction has the stable spectrum of $A-GX$. Any generalized eigenvector of the displayed triangular matrix for a stable eigenvalue has trailing component in the kernel of a power of $(-(A-GX)^* -\lambda I)$; that matrix is invertible because the trailing spectrum is in the open right half-plane, so the trailing component is zero. By [F6] these generalized eigenspaces have total dimension equal to the stable algebraic multiplicity $n$ from [F5], so they fill the first coordinate subspace, which is therefore the stable invariant subspace. The solution satisfies $R+B^*XB\succ0$, and its closed loop $A_c=A-B(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA$ is Schur stable. For each $x_0$, the infinite-horizon discrete cost
$$\inf_{(u_k)}\sum_{k=0}^\infty(x_k^*Qx_k+u_k^*Ru_k),\qquad x_{k+1}=Ax_k+Bu_k,$$
over sequences with finite cost equals $x_0^*Xx_0$ and is attained by $u_k=-K_dx_k$. Singular $A$ is allowed throughout; no inverse of $A$ is used.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $A\in F^{n\times n}$, $B\in F^{n\times m}$, $C\in F^{p\times n}$, and $R=R^*\in F^{m\times m}$ be positive definite. Write $Q=C^*C$ and $G=BR^{-1}B^*$. The inverse $R^{-1}$ is well-defined: [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]] supplies an invertible factor $R=LL^*$, so $R^{-1}=L^{-*}L^{-1}$. Thus $v^*Gv=\|L^{-1}B^*v\|_2^2\ge0$ and $v^*Qv=\|Cv\|_2^2\ge0$. The symbol $^*$ is transpose over $\mathbb R$ and conjugate transpose over $\mathbb C$.

The **continuous algebraic Riccati equation (CARE)** is
$$A^*X+XA-XGX+Q=0.$$
Its residual is $F_c(X)=A^*X+XA-XGX+Q$, its feedback is $K_c(X)=R^{-1}B^*X$, and its closed-loop matrix is $A_c(X)=A-BK_c(X)=A-GX$.

For $X=X^*\succeq0$, $S_X:=R+B^*XB$ is positive definite because
$v^*S_Xv=v^*Rv+(Bv)^*X(Bv)>0$ for every nonzero $v$. The **discrete
algebraic Riccati equation (DARE)** is
$$X=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA.$$
Its residual is $F_d(X)=Q+A^*XA-A^*XB(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA-X$. Whenever $X=X^*$, the matrix $R+B^*XB$ is positive definite if $X\succeq0$. Its feedback and closed-loop matrix are
$$K_d(X)=(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA,\qquad A_c(X)=A-BK_d(X).$$
A CARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian and $A_c(X)$ is Hurwitz. A DARE solution is **stabilizing** when it is Hermitian, $R+B^*XB\succ0$, and $A_c(X)$ is Schur stable. No inverse of $A$ is part of either definition.

For Hermitian $X$ with $S_X$ invertible, multiplication gives
$$(I+GX)^{-1}=I-BS_X^{-1}B^*X,\qquad X(I+GX)^{-1}=X-XB S_X^{-1}B^*X.$$
In either product, the additional coefficient of $B$ is
$R^{-1}-S_X^{-1}-S_X^{-1}(B^*XB)R^{-1}=0$, because
$S_X=R+B^*XB$. Thus the DARE is equivalently
$X=Q+A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}A$, and its closed-loop matrix is
$A_c(X)=(I+GX)^{-1}A$.

The associated homogeneous symplectic pencil is
$$N=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\-Q&I\end{bmatrix},\qquad M=\begin{bmatrix}I&G\\0&A^*\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathcal P(\alpha,\beta)=\beta N-\alpha M.$$
The homogeneous-coordinate convention is that a finite eigenvalue
$\lambda$ is $[\alpha:\beta]=[\lambda:1]$ and $[1:0]$ denotes infinity.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real or complex inner product space and let
$T:V\to V$ be non-negative. Then there exists a unique non-negative operator
$R:V\to V$ such that

$$R^2=T.$$

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathbb F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let
$A,B\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$. The **matrix pencil** determined by $(A,B)$ is
$A-\lambda B$. Its determinant polynomial is
$f(\lambda)=\det(A-\lambda B)$, with real coefficients viewed as complex
coefficients when $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$. The pencil is **regular** if $f$ is
not the zero polynomial; otherwise it is **singular**.

For $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$ not both zero, put
$$p(\alpha,\beta)=\det(\beta A-\alpha B).$$
A **homogeneous generalized eigenvalue pair** is an equivalence class of such
pairs satisfying $p(\alpha,\beta)=0$, where $(\alpha,\beta)$ and
$(c\alpha,c\beta)$ represent the same pair for every $c\in\mathbb C\setminus
\{0\}$. If $\beta\ne0$, the associated finite generalized eigenvalue is
$\lambda=\alpha/\beta$; if $\beta=0$, the pair is an infinite generalized
eigenvalue. The pair $(0,0)$ is never an eigenvalue pair.
Write $\sigma(A,B)$ for the set of finite ratios $\alpha/\beta$ among these
homogeneous eigenvalue pairs.

The QZ results on this page assume a regular pencil. They make no assertion
about Kronecker structure or eigenvalues of a singular pencil.

For $n\ge1$ and $A,B\in M_n(R)$ over a commutative ring,
$$\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B).$$

If $A=(a_{ij})\in M_n(R)$ is upper or lower triangular over a commutative ring, with $n\ge1$, then
$$\det(A)=\prod_{i<n}a_{ii}.$$

Let $n_1,n_2\ge1$, $n=n_1+n_2$, and let $A,B\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ be
block upper triangular with the same two-block partition of sizes $n_1,n_2$,
with diagonal blocks $A_{11},A_{22}$ and
$B_{11},B_{22}$. For every $\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C$,
$$\det(\beta A-\alpha B) =\det(\beta A_{11}-\alpha B_{11})\det(\beta A_{22}-\alpha B_{22}).$$

For an endomorphism $T$ of a finite-dimensional $F$-vector space,

$$\sigma_F(T)=\{\lambda\in F:\chi_T(\lambda)=0\}.$$
Every nonconstant polynomial in $\mathbb C[x]$ splits over $\mathbb C$.
Every endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space over an algebraically closed field has a Jordan canonical form over that field, including the endomorphism of the zero space.

derivations.claim: The matrix $I+GX$ is invertible. Indeed, if $(I+GX)v=0$, multiplication by $v^*X$ gives $v^*Xv+(Xv)^*G(Xv)=0.$ Both summands are nonnegative. By [F3], $v^*Xv=0$ implies $Xv=0$, and the original equation then gives $v=0$. Also $S=R+B^*XB\succ0$ by [F1]. The identity $(I+GX)^{-1}=I-BS^{-1}B^*X$ is verified by multiplying the right side by $I+GX$: the extra term is $B[R^{-1}-S^{-1}-S^{-1}(B^*XB)R^{-1}]B^*X=0$, since $S=R+B^*XB$. Therefore $A_c=(I+GX)^{-1}A$.

The DARE and the identity in step 1.1 imply $X-Q=A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}A=A^*XA_c$. Consequently, $N\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}A\\X-Q\end{bmatrix} =\begin{bmatrix}I+GX\\A^*X\end{bmatrix}A_c =M\begin{bmatrix}I\\X\end{bmatrix}A_c.$ This proves the deflating graph identity.

Put $T_X=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\X&I\end{bmatrix}$ and $L_X=\begin{bmatrix}I&0\\-A^*X(I+GX)^{-1}&I\end{bmatrix}$. By [F6] both are block triangular with identity diagonal and determinant one. For arbitrary homogeneous coordinates $[\alpha:\beta]$, $L_X(\beta N-\alpha M)T_X= \begin{bmatrix} (I+GX)(\beta A_c-\alpha I)&-\alpha G\\ 0&\beta I-\alpha A_c^* \end{bmatrix}.$ The lower-left block vanishes by $X-Q=A^*XA_c$; the lower-right block uses $(I+GX)^{-1}G=G(I+XG)^{-1}$ and $I-X(I+GX)^{-1}G=(I+XG)^{-1}$. Taking determinants and using [F5] and [F7] gives $\det(\beta N-\alpha M)=\det(I+GX)\det(\beta A_c-\alpha I)\det(\beta I-\alpha A_c^*).$ The first homogeneous factor has $n$ roots, counted with multiplicity; all are finite and equal to eigenvalues of $A_c$, hence strictly inside the disk by [F1] and [F8]. The roots of $A_c^*$ are the conjugates of those of $A_c$, since $\det(\mu I-A_c^*)=\overline{\det(\overline\mu I-A_c)}$; hence each nonzero eigenvalue of $A_c^*$ has modulus less than one. The second factor has $n$ roots, counted with multiplicity: each finite root is the reciprocal of a nonzero eigenvalue of $A_c^*$ and therefore has modulus greater than one, while every zero eigenvalue of $A_c^*$ contributes a root at $\beta=0$, which is infinite. The root counts follow from [F9], with finite eigenvalues identified by [F8]. Neither factor vanishes on $|\alpha|=|\beta|$, so the pencil is regular with the stated root split. The homogeneous determinant is invariant under these transforms because [F5] gives multiplicativity and both shear determinants equal one by [F6]. Finally, $(I+GX)$ is invertible by step 1.1, so $M[I;X]$ has full column rank. A Jordan basis of $A_c$ from [F10], together with $N[I;X]=M[I;X]A_c$ from step 2.1, shows that the graph carries all $n$ stable finite root chains; the determinant factorization shows there are exactly $n$ stable roots in total, so this is the stable deflating graph. This uses no inverse of $A$.

Inputs are CARE data with $Q=C^*C\succeq0$, $R\succ0$, a supplied stabilizing gain $K_0$, a nonnegative integer outer budget $N$, and either exact or safeguarded-inexact solve mode. Each exact-mode pass takes an admissible control packet for [[alg-bartels-stewart-sylvester-equation]]: pivot threshold $\tau_{\rm BS}\ge0$, a fixed $c_0>0$, nonnegative integer Schur sweep budgets $N_A,N_B\le c_0n$, and Schur controls for each coefficient matrix (deflation tolerance, positive integer stagnation period, finite exceptional-shift tables, arithmetic/range controls, and any supplied encoding or evaluator). Use its bounded-controller mode with a supplied nonnegative integer instruction budget $K_{\rm BS}$ and its built-in discriminant-sign controller. In inexact mode, also supply a nonnegative integer line-search limit $L$; each pass takes a Hermitian proposal $\widetilde P_j$, a stored candidate $\widehat X_j$ and approximate inverses for the finite Lyapunov systems below, and finite factorization witnesses for each trial. Stored inputs and point-solve proposals in this mode are exact dyadics; derived gains and coefficients are retained as exact rational expressions. Every point call uses the operationwise controller of [[alg-point-verified-linear-system-certifier]]; every scalar enclosure uses a finite outward evaluator with a declared work budget. Write $S(K)=Q+K^*RK$ and $\mathcal L_A(P)=A^*P+PA$.

For $j=0,\ldots,N-1$, put $A_j=A-BK_j$. In exact mode, call [[alg-bartels-stewart-sylvester-equation]] with coefficient matrices $A_j^*,A_j$, right-hand side $-S(K_j)$, and that pass's complete control packet to solve
$$\mathcal L_{A_j}(X_j)=-S(K_j).$$
If it does not return success, stop with its status. Otherwise set $K_{j+1}=R^{-1}B^*X_j$, append the gain and residual, and continue.

In safeguarded-inexact mode, $X_j$ denotes the unique exact solution of $\mathcal L_{A_j}(X_j)=-S(K_j)$; it exists because $K_0$ is stabilizing and every previously accepted trial has a Hurwitz witness. Under column vectorization, use the point matrix $I_n\otimes A_j^*+A_j^T\otimes I_n$ for $\mathcal L_{A_j}$, as in [[lem-sylvester-vectorization-isometry-and-kronecker-identity]]. Before the current-cost point call, clear a common positive integer denominator $d_j$ from this exact rational coefficient matrix and from $-\operatorname{vec}(S(K_j))$. Call [[alg-point-verified-linear-system-certifier]] on the resulting dyadic system, with the supplied inverse proposal for the scaled coefficient and $\widehat X_j$ as the solution proposal. Scaling both sides by $d_j$ preserves the exact solution $X_j$; if the scaled entries cannot be stored exactly in the declared point format, return `range-failure`. A `range-failure` returns that status; an `inconclusive` result returns `safeguard-inconclusive`. Let its solution ball have center $\widehat X_j$ and radius $s_j$, replacing the center by its Hermitian part if needed. Set $D_j=\widetilde P_j-\widehat X_j$ and compute the outward Gershgorin upper bound
$$\eta_j=s_j+\max_i\left((D_j)_{ii}+\sum_{k\ne i}|(D_j)_{ik}|\right).$$
For Hermitian $D_j$, the maximum row bound above is at least $\lambda_{\max}(D_j)$, by applying the eigenvector equation at a coordinate of maximal modulus. Define $\widetilde K_j=R^{-1}B^*\widetilde P_j$ and inspect the finite line-search list $\theta_\ell=2^{-\ell}$, $0\le\ell\le L$. For each trial $K_\ell=K_j+\theta_\ell(\widetilde K_j-K_j)$, let $A_\ell=A-BK_\ell$ and use its supplied exact factor witnesses $W_\ell=L_\ell^*L_\ell$ with nonsingular $L_\ell$, and $Z_\ell$ satisfying
$$A_\ell^*W_\ell+W_\ell A_\ell\preceq-\mu_\ell I,$$
where $\mu_\ell>0$ and $-A_\ell^*W_\ell-W_\ell A_\ell-\mu_\ell I=Z_\ell^*Z_\ell$. Verify these exact factor identities; otherwise reject the trial and continue. Vectorize $\mathcal L_{A_\ell}$ using the same coefficient matrix as for $A_j$. Outward-evaluate $I-R_\ell\mathcal L_{A_\ell}$ and let $q_\ell$ be a Frobenius upper bound. If no finite enclosure is available or $q_\ell\ge1$, reject the trial and continue. Set $\kappa_\ell=\|R_\ell\|_F/(1-q_\ell)$; the Neumann estimate and $\|T\|_2\le\|T\|_F$ give $\kappa_\ell\ge\|\mathcal L_{A_\ell}^{-1}\|_{F\to F}$. Separately outward-evaluate the raw residual and set $r_\ell$ to an upper bound for
$$\mathcal L_{A_\ell}(\widetilde P_j)+Q+K_\ell^*RK_\ell,$$
with Frobenius norm. Accept the first trial satisfying $\eta_j+\kappa_\ell r_\ell\le0$; then set $K_{j+1}=K_\ell$, append the accepted gain and its certificates, and proceed to pass $j+1$. If no trial passes, return `safeguard-inconclusive` without changing $K_j$. Any unavailable outward bound is inconclusive. The inverse bound above follows from the Neumann estimate, and $r_\ell$ bounds the raw residual separately; the preconditioned residual in [[def-verified-linear-residual-certificate-data]] is a different quantity. All certificate witnesses and bounds use the finite outward evaluator; a non-finite operation returns its range status. After at most $N$ accepted updates return the gain sequence, solve residuals, cost-matrix data and terminal status. An arbitrary approximate Lyapunov solve is never accepted without the separate stability and descent checks above.

The inverse $R^{-1}$ is well-defined: [[thm-cholesky-factorisation-exists-iff-hermitian-positive-definite-and-is-unique]] supplies an invertible factor $R=LL^*$, so $R^{-1}=L^{-*}L^{-1}$. $$K_d(X)=(R+B^*XB)^{-1}B^*XA,\qquad A_c(X)=A-BK_d(X).$$

For Hermitian $X$ with $S_X$ invertible, multiplication gives
$$(I+GX)^{-1}=I-BS_X^{-1}B^*X,\qquad X(I+GX)^{-1}=X-XB S_X^{-1}B^*X.$$

The associated homogeneous symplectic pencil is
$$N=\begin{bmatrix}A&0\\-Q&I\end{bmatrix},\qquad M=\begin{bmatrix}I&G\\0&A^*\end{bmatrix},\qquad \mathcal P(\alpha,\beta)=\beta N-\alpha M.$$
The homogeneous-coordinate convention is that a finite eigenvalue
$\lambda$ is $[\alpha:\beta]=[\lambda:1]$ and $[1:0]$ denotes infinity.

Let $A\in F^{n\times n}$ be Hurwitz and let $Q=Q^*\in F^{n\times n}$. Then the improper matrix integral

$$
X=\int_0^\infty e^{tA}Qe^{tA^*}\,dt
$$

converges and is the unique solution of $AX+XA^*+Q=0$. If $Q\succeq0$, then $X\succeq0$. If $Q\succ0$, then $X\succ0$. For $Q\succeq0$, $X\succ0$ if and only if there is no nonzero $v$ for which $e^{tA^*}v\in\ker Q^{1/2}$ for every $t\ge0$.

Let $F\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, $m,n\ge1$, $A\in F^{m\times m}$ and $B\in F^{n\times n}$. Spectra of real matrices are taken over $\mathbb C$. The map $\mathcal S_{A,B}$ of [[def-sylvester-operator-and-separation-number]] is invertible if and only if

$$
\sigma(A)\cap(-\sigma(B))=\varnothing.
$$

Equivalently, for every $C\in F^{m\times n}$, the equation $AX+XB=C$ has a unique solution if and only if this spectral condition holds. The same condition is equivalent to $\operatorname{sep}(A,-B)>0$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal A$ be a nonempty set of matrices in $\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, and let $\mathcal b$ be a nonempty subset of $\mathbb C^n$. A **uniform residual certificate** consists of a point matrix $R\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, a point vector $\widehat x\in\mathbb C^n$, and numbers $q,r\ge0$ such that
$$
\|I-RA\|_2\le q,\qquad \|R(b-A\widehat x)\|_2\le r
$$
for every $A\in\mathcal A$ and $b\in\mathcal b$. Here $\|\cdot\|_2$ is the operator norm induced by the Euclidean vector norm, as in [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]]. The certificate is **usable** when $q<1$; in that case its reported error radius is $r/(1-q)$. The point-data case is $\mathcal A=\{A\}$ and $\mathcal b=\{b\}$.

This definition specifies mathematical upper bounds; it does not specify how a computation establishes them.

derivations.claim: If $A_tv=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$, the certificate gives $2\operatorname{Re}(\lambda)v^*Wv=v^*(A_t^*W+WA_t)v\le-\mu\|v\|_2^2<0.$ Because $W\succ0$, every eigenvalue has negative real part, so $A_t$ is Hurwitz.

Let $P_t$ be the exact solution of the Lyapunov equation; it exists uniquely by [F3] and [F4], and $P_t\succeq0$ by [F2]–[F3]. If $R_t$ denotes the exact residual of $\widetilde P$, then $\mathcal L_{A_t}(\widetilde P-P_t)=R_t$. The Statement's certified inverse and raw residual bounds give $\|\widetilde P-P_t\|_F\le\kappa r$; these are distinct from the certificate quantities described in [F5]. For each unit vector $v$, $v^*(P_t-X_j)v\le v^*(\widetilde P-X_j)v+\|P_t-\widetilde P\|_2\le\eta+\kappa r\le0.$ Thus $P_t\preceq X_j$.
